A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Skip-It? framework and share substantial theory and experiments. Their complete main text and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: Sections 4–5 and Appendices C–D report original hidden-state redundancy, attention and layer-skipping experiments across multiple VLMs and datasets.

after.justification: The retained experiments are supplemented with original captioning results, spectral-norm measurements, CKA analyses and calibration-subset comparisons.

M1.justification: V1 provides redundancy criteria and skipping sweeps; v2 introduces an explicit selection procedure in Algorithm 1. It uses an unlabeled calibration subset and threshold tests to select contiguous initial and terminal blocks for late entry and early exit, adding an operational algorithm to the framework.

E1.justification: V2 adds image captioning on COCO and Flickr30k, extending evaluation from question answering and reasoning to open-ended description generation (Table 3, Tables 1–2 and Figures 16–17). The original QA, OCR and reasoning datasets remain.

E2.justification: The performance comparisons remain skipping configurations versus the corresponding unskipped backbone. Qwen's new skipping results extend backbone configurations; cited methods such as Skip-Vision, ST3 and SAINT are not added as experimentally evaluated competitors.

E3.justification: V2 adds BLEU, CIDEr and SPICE evaluation for captioning, CKA-based redundancy checks, and full-dataset versus 100- and 1,000-example comparisons in Figure 19. NeXT figure labels also change from Vicuna to Mistral, although matching retained curves and scores do not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses examine Lipschitz-assumption plausibility through spectral norms (Appendix A.4), robustness to the representation-similarity metric through CKA (Figure 18), and calibration-subset representativeness (Appendix D). These questions were not tested in v1.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, empirical confidence intervals or significance tests. V2's subset overlays compare sample sizes without estimating uncertainty, and its new Hoeffding bound is a theoretical result.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 add Qwen skipping results and captioning scores; for example, v2 reports Qwen General VQA accuracy of 0.823 without skipping and 0.587 at late-entry layer 4. Shared LLaVA accuracy entries remain unchanged. Separate 'guessing' summary rows disappear, and Table 2 replaces geometric/proximal summaries with VAR values.

T1.justification: V2 replaces the discrete Fano formulation with a continuous version, revises Theorems 4–5 and adds a conditional-entropy corollary. Appendix A.2 adds late-entry and early-exit error bounds and a Hoeffding generalization theorem. The existing PID definitions and proof are retained in Appendix A.3.

C1.justification: V2 makes selection from a small unlabeled calibration subset an explicit main contribution and claims a bridge to practical deployment. It also extends the existing unification claim toward token pruning, while retaining the central claim that redundancy conditions predict viable layer skipping.

C2.justification: V1 emphasizes similar redundancy across datasets and shared processing across models. V2 instead highlights task dependence and proposes query complexity as an explanation for captioning/VQA differences. Sections 3.3–3.4 also acknowledge the limited usefulness of informational redundancy for deterministic layer transitions and qualify implications involving differential entropy.

D1.justification: Algorithm 1 adds procedural documentation of calibration inputs, per-layer quantities and threshold-based layer searches; Appendix A.4 specifies spectral-norm estimation. The original answer-generation and GPT-5 judging instructions remain unchanged. No code-access or hardware information is added.

R1.justification: Sections 2.2, 4.1 and 5 substantially expand positioning around unifying pruning methods, discussing Skip-Vision, ST3, SAINT and Shukor and Cord. The separate interpretability review and several associated citations are removed. These changes go beyond bibliographic updates to retained works.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, framework explanations and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Separate validation and performance sections become a unified Section 4 followed by a dedicated Discussion, and PID material moves into the theory appendix. The narrative shifts toward operational selection and broader pruning applications.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column main-text layout, reorganizes figure panels and structurally expands Tables 1–2. The original combined VAR figure becomes separate task-level plots, while spectral-norm, captioning, CKA and calibration figures are added. Existing diagrams and many appendix plots are retained and relocated.

improvement.justification: Captioning evidence and the qualifications concerning deterministic layers and differential entropy make v2's conclusions better scoped; CKA and calibration studies add useful support. However, the new deployment claim remains incompletely supported: Algorithm 1 has no reported end-to-end evaluation, and its late-entry rule omits the cross-modal control assumed in Theorem 6. These gaps limit the net quality gain despite the substantial revision.
